body.statement: If \(D\neq\varnothing\), the identified set of \(b=P(Y_0=0,Y_1=1)\) over \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cl}}\) is exactly \([L,U]\). Each endpoint is attained by the construction in \(\mathrm{def:attaining-law}\). For each fixed odds endpoint, \(C_{\theta}\) is complete and contains at most ten distinct channels: at most five vertices, at most four axis-edge contacts with the two stationary lines, and at most one stationary point on \(v-u=\kappa\). Without the informativeness cut, at most eight channels suffice.
body.justification: This is the theorem-level kernel: a nonlinear sharp set becomes a constant-size, closed-form candidate map with constructive attainment.
body.gap: ZhangNieSoonLiu2013 fixes clean margins and Molinari2008 leaves general channel restrictions to nonlinear programming; neither supplies the shared-channel stationary-line completeness theorem.
body.consumer: A validation-enabled trial analyst can compute sharp benefit bounds without trusting a generic nonlinear optimizer at feasibility edges.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(x=q_0\), \(y=q_1\), \(\delta=y-x\), and \(d=v-u\).  The channel polygon \(D\) is a closed rectangle intersected with one closed half-plane.  It is therefore compact and convex, and it has at most five vertices.  For fixed \(\theta\), multiply the root equation by \(d^2>0\) to obtain
\[
 H(u,v,b)=r d^2b^2+(d-r\delta)d b-(y-u)(v-x)=0.
\]
The unique-root lemma gives
\[
 H_b=d^2\{\theta(p_{01}+p_{10})+p_{11}+p_{00}\}>0.
\]
Thus along every line segment in \(D\), implicit differentiation is legitimate away from an endpoint, including when \(\theta=1\).

First exclude unlisted interior extrema.  If \(x\neq y\), the map \((u,v)\mapsto(p_0,p_1)\) has Jacobian determinant
\[
 \det\frac{\partial(p_0,p_1)}{\partial(u,v)}=\frac{y-x}{(v-u)^3}\neq0.
\]
At an interior channel, all four compatible cells are positive: both margins are strictly between zero and one, and a finite positive \(\theta\) places the unique root strictly inside its Fr\'echet interval.  Hence the two margin derivatives in the comparative-statics lemma are respectively strictly negative and strictly positive.  Their gradient cannot be annihilated by an invertible Jacobian, so no interior stationary point exists.  If \(x=y=q\), then \(p_0=p_1=p\), and the equation becomes
\[
 rb^2+b=p(1-p),\qquad
 \frac{db}{dp}=\frac{1-2p}{1+2rb}.
\]
The denominator equals the positive root derivative.  The only interior stationary set is therefore \(p=1/2\), equivalently \(u+v=2q\), and on it
\[
 b=\frac{1}{2(1+\sqrt\theta)}.
\]
If this ridge meets \(D\), the endpoints of its intersection with the compact polygon lie on the boundary and are listed by the candidate rule: they are stationary-line contacts on axis-aligned edges or the single central contact on the informativeness edge.

It remains to classify each boundary edge.  Direct differentiation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_u&=-2rdb^2-(2d-r\delta)b+v-x,\\
H_v&= 2rdb^2+(2d-r\delta)b-(y-u),\\
H_u+H_v&=u+v-x-y.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(r\neq0\), elementary polynomial elimination of \(b\) gives the factorizations
\[
\operatorname{Res}_b(H,H_u)
=-r^2d^2(v-x)(v-y)\{\theta\delta^2-(u+v-x-y)^2\},
\]
\[
\operatorname{Res}_b(H,H_v)
=-r^2d^2(u-x)(u-y)\{\theta\delta^2-(u+v-x-y)^2\}.
\]
These identities follow by expanding the two quadratic--linear resultants; hence a common zero makes the displayed product zero.  On a horizontal edge, stationarity in its varying \(u\)-coordinate requires \(H_u=0\); away from a margin contact all prefactors are nonzero, so
\[
 u+v=x+y\pm\sqrt\theta\,|y-x|.
\]
The identical conclusion follows on a vertical edge from \(H_v=0\).  When \(r=0\), direct differentiation of
\[
 b=\frac{(y-u)(v-x)}{(v-u)^2}
\]
gives
\[
 b_u=\frac{(v-x)(2y-u-v)}{(v-u)^3},
 \qquad
 b_v=\frac{(y-u)(2x-u-v)}{(v-u)^3};
\]
the two stationary lines are \(u+v=2y\) and \(u+v=2x\), exactly the preceding formula at \(\theta=1\).

The excluded margin-contact edges have no hidden extremum.  If \(x\leq y\), then on \(u=x\) one has \(b=(y-x)/(v-x)\), and on \(v=y\) one has \(b=(y-x)/(y-u)\); each is monotone along the edge.  If \(y\leq x\), then on \(u=y\) or \(v=x\) one has \(b=0\).  Equal-risk contact edges likewise have \(b=0\).  Their extrema are therefore at vertices.  Finally, on \(v=u+\kappa\), implicit differentiation and the formula for \(H_u+H_v\) give
\[
 \frac{d}{du}b_{\theta}(u,u+\kappa)
 =-\frac{2u+\kappa-x-y}{H_b}.
\]
There is at most one stationary point, and it is the listed point \(u+v=x+y\).  Vertices cover the remaining endpoints.  The same one-dimensional argument covers a segment, and a singleton is itself a vertex.  This proves candidate completeness.

For the count, intersecting a rectangle with the half-plane \(v-u\geq\kappa\) produces at most five vertices.  Each of the two distinct-or-coincident slope \(-1\) stationary lines intersects the boundary of a convex polygon in at most two points; because it cannot coincide with an axis-aligned or slope \(1\) edge, it contributes at most two axis-edge contacts.  The informativeness edge contributes at most one further stationary point.  After duplicates are removed,
\[
 |C_{\theta}|\leq5+4+1=10.
\]
If the informativeness cut is absent, the feasible polygon is a rectangle, so the corresponding count is \(4+4=8\).

The comparative-statics lemma profiles the odds coordinate: the minimum over \(\theta\in[\theta_L,\theta_U]\) is at \(\theta_U\), and the maximum is at \(\theta_L\).  Candidate completeness and the definition of \(L,U\) therefore identify the extrema of the continuous root map over \(D\times[\theta_L,\theta_U]\).

It remains to prove sharpness rather than merely an outer bound.  For every \((u,v,\theta)\) in that domain, the unique-root lemma makes the four masses in the attaining-law definition nonnegative, summing to one, and satisfying
\[
 p_{11}p_{00}=\theta p_{10}p_{01},
\]
which implies the closed cross-product band.  Conditional Bernoulli generation of \(W_a\) gives sensitivity \(v=s\) and specificity \(1-u=c\); independent randomization and consistency give the observed risks by assay inversion.  Hence every root value is attained by a law in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cl}}\).  Conversely, every law in that model supplies a channel in \(D\), and its closed band supplies some \(\theta\in[\theta_L,\theta_U]\): if \(p_{10}p_{01}>0\), take \(\theta=p_{11}p_{00}/(p_{10}p_{01})\); if the product is zero, the closed inequalities force \(p_{11}p_{00}=0\), so any band value gives the equality.  Uniqueness then makes its benefit equal to the compatible root.

Finally, any two domain points are joined by a line segment in the convex set \(D\times[\theta_L,\theta_U]\).  Along that segment the root is continuous.  The supremum construction used in the unique-root proof, applied to the continuous scalar path, shows that every value between its endpoint values is taken.  Joining minimizers and maximizers therefore shows that the attainable image is exactly \([L,U]\).  This proves both sharpness and endpoint attainment by the stated construction.
